paragraphs.title: The Destruction of Damascus and Ephraim

easy.explanation: Isaiah 17:1 says that Damascus shall be taken away from being a city and shall be a ruinous heap.
easy.q: What is Damascus said to become?

easy.explanation: The cities of Aroer shall be forsaken and shall be for flocks.
easy.q: Who will lie down in the cities of Aroer?

easy.explanation: The verse says, “The fortress also shall cease from Ephraim.”

answers: They are all promised greater strength
They are all connected with decline and destruction
They are all spared from judgment
medium.explanation: The passage describes the fall of Damascus, the remnant of Syria, and the loss of Ephraim’s fortress and kingdom.
medium.q: What do Damascus, Syria, and Ephraim have in common in this prophecy?

medium.explanation: A ruinous heap is a place reduced to ruins.
medium.q: What does “ruinous heap” mean in the context of Damascus?

medium.explanation: The cities are forsaken, and flocks lie down there without anyone making them afraid.
medium.q: What does the abandonment of the cities of Aroer show?

answers: Flocks lying down with none to make them afraid
Mighty waters rushing through the streets
challenge.explanation: The peaceful flocks show that the cities have been deserted.
challenge.q: What picture emphasizes the silence and abandonment of the cities of Aroer?

answers: Their glory and status will decline
They will become stronger than Israel
challenge.explanation: In this context, the comparison points to a reduction of their former glory and strength.
challenge.q: What is suggested by Syria and Damascus becoming “as the glory of the children of Israel”?

answers: Damascus is ruined, cities are forsaken, and political strength collapses
Cities prosper, harvests increase, and kingdoms expand
New fortresses are built and the people celebrate
challenge.explanation: The passage moves from Damascus’s ruin to abandoned cities and the loss of fortresses and kingdoms.
challenge.q: What is the main sequence of events in these verses?

easy.explanation: Isaiah says that “the glory of Jacob shall be made thin.”
easy.q: What will happen to the glory of Jacob?

answers: A field or grove with only a small remainder
easy.explanation: Jacob is compared to a harvest and an olive tree from which only a few remnants remain.
easy.q: What is Jacob compared to after the harvest?

easy.explanation: The verse says, “two or three berries in the top of the uppermost bough.”
easy.q: How many berries may remain in the topmost bough?

answers: They both describe a small remainder after gathering
They both describe the building of cities
medium.explanation: Both images show that most has been taken away, leaving only a few remnants.
medium.q: What do the pictures of the harvest and the olive tree have in common?

answers: Grapes left behind after the main gathering
medium.explanation: Gleaning grapes are grapes that remain after the main harvest has been gathered.

answers: Most of the crop is gathered, leaving only remnants
The crop grows after it has been gathered
medium.explanation: The harvestman gathers the corn, while only a few ears remain afterward.
medium.q: What process is described by the harvest image?

answers: Jacob will remain wealthy but hidden
Jacob will lose much of his glory and resources
Jacob will begin planting new groves
challenge.explanation: The few remaining stalks and berries picture severe loss and poverty.
challenge.q: What is the main meaning of the field and olive-tree images concerning Jacob?

answers: Two or three berries and four or five branches
challenge.explanation: The very small numbers show how little will remain after the gathering.
challenge.q: Which detail most strongly emphasizes how small the remainder will be?

answers: Both describe an increase of abundance
Both describe becoming emptied and diminished
Both describe a time of rest
challenge.explanation: Jacob’s body and the harvest are both portrayed as losing their former fullness.
challenge.q: How does “the fatness of his flesh shall wax lean” relate to the harvest image?

paragraphs.title: Turning to the Creator and Rejecting Human-Made Supports

answers: To the makers of the altars
easy.explanation: The verse says, “At that day shall a man look to his Maker.”
easy.q: To whom will a man look in that day?

answers: The altars and the work of his hands
easy.explanation: He will not look to the altars or respect the work made by his fingers.
easy.q: What will a man no longer trust in?

answers: They will result in grief and disappointing harvest
easy.explanation: Although the plants grow and flourish, the harvest becomes a heap in the day of grief.
easy.q: What will happen to the plantings described in these verses?

answers: Forgetting God is presented as the reason for the failure
medium.explanation: Because the people forgot the God of their salvation, their planting and labor would end in sorrow.
medium.q: What connection is made between forgetting God and the failure of the people’s efforts?

medium.explanation: Strong cities are fortified places intended to provide protection.
medium.q: What does “strong cities” mean in this passage?

answers: He no longer looks to it as a source of support
He turns it into a new altar
medium.explanation: He looks to his Maker instead of respecting the altars and images made by human hands.
medium.q: How does the man’s attitude toward the work of his hands change?

answers: Looking to the Creator versus rejecting human-made supports
challenge.explanation: The passage contrasts respect for the Holy One of Israel with reliance on human-made altars and images.
challenge.q: What central contrast appears in these verses?

answers: A promising beginning does not guarantee a good result
The plant never grew at all
challenge.explanation: The plant grows during the day and flourishes in the morning, yet the final harvest brings grief.
challenge.q: What can be inferred from a plant that flourishes but produces a sorrowful harvest?

answers: A movement from trust in God to trust in idols
A movement from human supports to the Creator
A movement from farming to city building
challenge.explanation: The people turn away from the work of their hands and look to their Maker.

paragraphs.title: The Roar of the Nations and the Enemy’s Defeat

answers: The noise of the seas and mighty waters
easy.explanation: The nations make a noise like the noise of the seas and the rushing of mighty waters.
easy.q: What is the noise of the nations compared to?

answers: It makes them flee far off
It hides them in a city
easy.explanation: God rebukes them, and they flee far off.
easy.q: What does God’s rebuke do to the threatening nations?

easy.explanation: The passage says, “before the morning he is not.”
easy.q: When is the enemy no longer present?

answers: From threatening noise to scattering and disappearance
medium.explanation: The nations appear powerful and loud, but God’s rebuke causes them to flee and vanish.
medium.q: What is the main movement in these verses?

medium.explanation: Rushing describes the forceful movement and sound of the waters.
medium.q: What does “rushing” mean in the phrase “the rushing of mighty waters”?

answers: Chaff before the wind and a rolling thing before the whirlwind
medium.explanation: The nations are chased like chaff before the wind and like a rolling thing before the whirlwind.
medium.q: What images are used for the enemy’s flight?

answers: The nations look terrifying but cannot withstand God’s rebuke
The nations are stronger than the wind
The nations remain in place for a long time
challenge.explanation: Though the nations seem powerful, God quickly drives them away.
challenge.q: What does the contrast between mighty waters and scattered chaff emphasize?

answers: Trouble appears in the evening, but the enemy is gone before morning
Joy changes to sorrow at midday
Silence changes to noise after sunrise
challenge.explanation: The enemy causes trouble at evening, but disappears before the morning.
challenge.q: How does the situation change during the night?

answers: The enemies’ appointed fate is defeat and disappearance
It describes the reward of the defenders
challenge.explanation: The final verse declares that this scattering and disappearance will be the fate of those who plunder and rob.
challenge.q: What does “the portion of them that spoil us, and the lot of them that rob us” mean?
